title: The cache directives
summary: Which directive keeps the bytes off the disk, which one only makes a cache ask first, and what a hard reload is really sending.

sources.author: web.dev
sources.title: Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache

cards.front: Which of `no-store` and `no-cache` keeps the response off the disk, and what does the other one do instead?
cards.back: `no-store`. RFC 9111: a cache "MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response", private and shared alike. `no-cache` stores it and revalidates before each reuse, even when the cache is disconnected from the origin, so a copy on disk is the expected state. One of the two names is a lie, and it is `no-cache`.

cards.front: `no-cache` and `max-age=0`. What is the difference, and which one used to be spelled as the other?
cards.back: `max-age=0` is stale on arrival; `no-cache` may never be reused without asking first. Stale is not forbidden, which is why `no-cache` was once written `max-age=0, must-revalidate`. MDN calls that pairing "a remnant" of implementations predating HTTP/1.1 and says there is "no reason to ever use" it now. Write `no-cache`.

cards.front: The dashboard is personalised. Which directive keeps it out of a shared cache, and does that keep it off the laptop?
cards.back: `private`, and no. It narrows storage to the browser rather than preventing it, so the copy still lands on disk. `no-cache` will not save you either: it is a freshness control, not a privacy one. If the requirement is that these bytes must not survive on this machine, the directive is `no-store`.

cards.front: You shipped `no-store` and the old value keeps coming back. What did the header not do?
cards.back: Evict. MDN: "if there is an old response already stored for a particular URL, returning `no-store` will not prevent the old response from being reused." The directive stops a response being written and says nothing about what is already written, so it fixes the future and not the present. A new URL does, and so does a revalidation the stored copy has to pass.

cards.front: A hashed bundle, the HTML that names it, and a bank statement. One `Cache-Control` line each.
cards.back: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, then `no-cache`, then `no-store`. The asset's name changes when its bytes do, so it can never be wrong. The HTML is cheap to check and must never be a version behind. web.dev recommends the first two directly: a year for URLs carrying a fingerprint, `no-cache` with a validator for the ones that do not.

cards.front: What does `no-store` on every response cost you, and what does MDN recommend as the default instead?
cards.back: The 304 that would have cost nothing. Nothing is stored, so the hashed bundle is downloaded again on every navigation. MDN's advice runs the other way: "prefer the use of `no-cache` in combination with `private`", which keeps the copy and checks it rather than throwing it away and refetching it in full.

cards.front: A reload and a hard reload. What does the browser send for each, and which one can come back as a 304?
cards.back: A reload sends `Cache-Control: max-age=0` with `If-None-Match` and `If-Modified-Since`, so a 304 is a successful reload that transferred nothing. A hard reload sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Pragma: no-cache` with no conditions, so it is a 200 from the origin, body and all. MDN documents those headers for Chrome, Edge and Firefox; Safari differs a little.

cards.front: "It works when I hard reload." What has that told you, and why does it not close the ticket?
cards.back: It tells you the stale copy was above the network line, which is worth knowing and takes one keystroke. It is not a fix, because it is you sending `Cache-Control: no-cache` for one navigation in one browser, and nobody else visiting the site is going to do it.
